questions.statement: Which structure is most appropriate for an argumentative essay?
questions.context: A student receives an assignment to write an argumentative essay of five paragraphs.

options.text: An introduction with the position, body paragraphs with evidence, and a conclusion.
options.feedback: Correct! An argument needs a claim, support and a closing statement of the result.

options.text: A single paragraph that states the opinion without explanation.
options.feedback: A single unsupported sentence is an assertion, not an argument.

options.text: A narrative that recounts a personal experience in order.
options.feedback: A personal narrative is a mode of narration, not a structure of argument.

options.text: A list of definitions with no position taken.
options.feedback: A list of definitions takes no position and supports no claim.

questions.explanation:
The structure of an argument is fixed: claim, development with evidence, and a conclusion that follows from what was argued.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is the strongest claim in an argumentative essay?
questions.context: A student must choose the central claim of an essay about school assessment.

options.text: The written exam has problems.
options.feedback: 'The written exam has problems' is vague because it does not say which problems.

options.text: Schools should replace the written exam with a portfolio of work.
options.feedback: Correct! The sentence states a clear, contestable position with a concrete proposal.

options.text: Exams exist.
options.feedback: 'Exams exist' is a fact that nobody disputes, so it cannot be argued.

options.text: Some students dislike exams.
options.feedback: 'Some students dislike exams' reports a reaction rather than making a claim.

questions.explanation:
A claim worth arguing is specific and open to disagreement. A claim that nobody would dispute cannot carry an argument.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which piece of evidence best supports a claim that longer class time improves results?
questions.context: A student gathers material for an essay arguing in favour of longer school days.

options.text: The opinion of the school principal.
options.feedback: An opinion is not evidence, and using one weakens the argument.

options.text: A description of what a classroom looks like.
options.feedback: A description of a room shows nothing about results.

options.text: A comparison of results in two schools with different timetables.
options.feedback: Correct! A comparison of results between two timetables is measurable evidence that can confirm or refute the claim.

options.text: A statement that students find long days tiring.
options.feedback: A statement about tiredness is an impression, and it may support the opposite claim.

questions.explanation:
Evidence has to be able to test the claim. Only data that could prove the claim wrong is useful support.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly presents a counterargument?
questions.context: A student introduces the strongest objection to the position defended in an essay.

options.text: Longer days are not always practical.
options.feedback: The first sentence expresses the writer's own doubt and weakens the position.

options.text: Some teachers prefer shorter days.
options.feedback: The second sentence is a personal preference and not a formulated argument.

options.text: Longer days need a timetable.
options.feedback: The third sentence is a practical note, not an opposing claim.

options.text: Critics point out that longer days reduce time for sport.
options.feedback: Correct! Naming the objectors and stating their point clearly is what presenting a counterargument means.

questions.explanation:
A counterargument must be stated at its strongest. Reporting it as what critics say keeps it separate from the writer's own position.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which connective best introduces a concession in an argument?
questions.context: A student acknowledges a point against a position before answering it in an essay.

options.text: Admittedly
options.feedback: Correct! 'Admittedly' signals that the writer accepts the opposing point for the sake of the argument.

options.text: Therefore
options.feedback: 'Therefore' presents a consequence and concedes nothing.

options.text: Moreover
options.feedback: 'Moreover' adds a supporting point and creates no concession.

options.text: Hence
options.feedback: 'Hence' is a result connective and likewise concedes nothing.

questions.explanation:
A concession must be visibly signalled, otherwise the reader cannot tell whether the sentence agrees or disagrees with the previous one.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which is the most suitable criterion for judging two arguments in an essay?
questions.context: A teacher explains how a student should compare two positions presented in a reading.

options.text: The number of words used to present them.
options.feedback: Length is not a measure of quality, and a long argument can still be weak.

options.text: The strength of the evidence and the quality of the reasoning.
options.feedback: Correct! Evidence and reasoning decide the strength of an argument; nothing else does.

options.text: The confidence with which the writer states the claim.
options.feedback: Confidence is a matter of tone and says nothing about the truth of a claim.

options.text: The order in which the arguments are presented.
options.feedback: The order of presentation is a matter of style, not of argument.

questions.explanation:
Judging an argument by its presentation rather than its support is a common error in reading exercises.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence states a limitation of a source in an argumentative essay?
questions.context: A student evaluates the usefulness of a survey before citing it in an essay.

options.text: The survey was published last year.
options.feedback: The date of publication is a fact about the source, not a limitation of its conclusions.

options.text: The survey contains forty questions.
options.feedback: The number of questions is a description of the instrument, not a weakness.

options.text: The survey covered only students from one school.
options.feedback: Correct! Restricting the sample to one school limits how far the results can be generalised.

options.text: The survey was carried out online.
options.feedback: The method of collection is a neutral detail unless it introduces a bias.

questions.explanation:
A limitation is a boundary that narrows what a source can prove. Other details describe the source without weakening it.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly acknowledges a counterargument and then refutes it?
questions.context: A student wants to present a concession and still defend the original position in a single sentence.

options.text: Longer days are tiring and I agree with that.
options.feedback: The first sentence abandons the original position instead of defending it.

options.text: Longer days are tiring, so the school should not change.
options.feedback: The second sentence gives in to the counterargument.

options.text: Longer days are tiring, and that is the main point.
options.feedback: The third sentence treats the objection as the writer's own claim.

options.text: Longer days are tiring, but the evidence on results outweighs that concern.
options.feedback: Correct! The sentence states the objection and then answers it, which is concession plus refutation in one structure.

questions.explanation:
A concession is only useful if it is answered. The connective after the concession marks the return to the position.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which phrase best introduces the main argument in a body paragraph?
questions.context: A student needs to open a paragraph that develops one of the reasons of an essay.

options.text: The central point is that
options.feedback: Correct! 'The central point is that' announces the claim the paragraph will develop.

options.text: Interestingly
options.feedback: 'Interestingly' comments on the material without introducing a claim.

options.text: In the end
options.feedback: 'In the end' belongs to a conclusion, not to a body paragraph.

options.text: At first
options.feedback: 'At first' belongs to an account of a sequence, not to an argument.

questions.explanation:
A topic sentence must contain the claim. Phrases that only comment or sequence leave the reader without a position to follow.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence best closes an argumentative essay?
questions.context: A student writes the final paragraph of an essay arguing for a change in the school timetable.

options.text: The change has many sides.
options.feedback: The first sentence is vague and closes nothing.

options.text: For these reasons, the change should be implemented next term.
options.feedback: Correct! The sentence gathers the reasons and repeats the position, which is the function of a conclusion.

options.text: Some people are worried about the change.
options.feedback: The third sentence reports a reaction that the essay was supposed to answer.

options.text: The change was discussed in three meetings.
options.feedback: The fourth sentence recounts a process and is not a conclusion.

questions.explanation:
A conclusion restates the claim in the light of the reasons given, so the reader leaves the essay with a clear position.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which verb is used to refer to evidence in academic argumentative writing?
questions.context: A student reviews the verbs used in a paragraph of a formal essay.

options.text: shout
options.feedback: 'Shout' is informal and unrelated to evidence.

options.text: happen
options.feedback: 'Happen' describes an event and does not take a clause as its object.

options.text: demonstrate
options.feedback: Correct! 'Demonstrate' means to show clearly that something holds, which is the function of evidence.

options.text: arrive
options.feedback: 'Arrive' describes movement towards a place and cannot introduce a claim.

questions.explanation:
Precise verbs carry the relationship between evidence and claim. A weak verb hides the link that the paragraph depends on.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence avoids presenting a personal preference as a general truth?
questions.context: A student writes about the conditions for revision and must keep the claims within the evidence.

options.text: Quiet is the best condition for study.
options.feedback: 'Quiet is the best' is an absolute claim with no evidence behind it.

options.text: I cannot concentrate with noise.
options.feedback: 'I cannot concentrate' is a single personal experience.

options.text: Study is best done in silence.
options.feedback: 'Study is best done in silence' generalises from an unstated basis.

options.text: Some students prefer quiet places, while others need noise to concentrate.
options.feedback: Correct! The sentence reports two preferences without claiming that either is universally better.

questions.explanation:
Generalising from a personal preference to everybody is the most common weakness in argumentative writing by students.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which structure best organises an essay that compares two positions and then chooses one?
questions.context: A student is asked to write an essay that evaluates two proposals and recommends one.

options.text: Present both positions fairly, weigh them with stated criteria and defend the choice.
options.feedback: Correct! Weighing two positions against declared criteria is what turns a comparison into a reasoned choice.

options.text: Present one position and ignore the other completely.
options.feedback: Ignoring one position produces an unbalanced essay that a reader will not accept.

options.text: Present the writer's position first and list the objections without answering them.
options.feedback: Listing objections without answering them leaves the position unsupported.

options.text: Alternate between the two positions sentence by sentence without a conclusion.
options.feedback: Alternating without a conclusion gives the reader no result at the end.

questions.explanation:
A comparative essay needs stated criteria. Without them the choice between the two positions is only a preference.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence states the outcome of an argument rather than a new point?
questions.context: A student writes the closing paragraph of an essay that has presented four arguments about the school day.

options.text: The shorter timetable saves time.
options.feedback: The first sentence states a benefit that could appear anywhere in the body.

options.text: Taken together, the evidence favours the shorter timetable.
options.feedback: Correct! The phrase 'taken together' shows that the sentence gathers the previous points instead of adding one.

options.text: A shorter timetable is convenient.
options.feedback: The third sentence is a single claim that still needs support.

options.text: Time is limited.
options.feedback: The fourth sentence is a general statement that closes nothing.

questions.explanation:
A conclusion is recognised by the reference it makes to the material already presented, not by its subject matter.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which phrase is the most precise way to attribute a claim in an essay?
questions.context: A student introduces a statistic into an essay and must show where it comes from.

options.text: Everybody knows the figure is rising.
options.feedback: 'Everybody knows' is not a source and claims agreement without evidence.

options.text: It is obvious that the figure is rising.
options.feedback: 'It is obvious' removes the need for evidence entirely.

options.text: According to the report published in 2019, the figure is rising.
options.feedback: Correct! The sentence names the source and the date, which is what attribution requires.

options.text: The figure is rising.
options.feedback: The last sentence states the claim with no source at all.

questions.explanation:
Attribution protects the writer. A claim with a named source can be checked, and a claim without one can only be doubted.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence would weaken an argument about the value of group work?
questions.context: A student checks which sentence would put a claim about group work in doubt.

options.text: Group work develops communication skills.
options.feedback: The first sentence supports the claim.

options.text: Group work requires careful planning.
options.feedback: The second sentence adds a condition that makes the claim more reasonable.

options.text: Some students prefer to work alone.
options.feedback: The third sentence is a fact that can be acknowledged in a balanced essay.

options.text: The research measured results after only four weeks.
options.feedback: Correct! A short measurement period limits what the results can show, so this sentence undermines the argument.

questions.explanation:
A weak point in the evidence for a claim can be used against it. A short study cannot demonstrate a lasting effect.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly states a requirement of an argumentative essay?
questions.context: A teacher explains to a class what a well-built argument requires.

options.text: Every claim should be supported by evidence or reasoning.
options.feedback: Correct! Support is what separates an argument from a sequence of opinions.

options.text: Every sentence should be longer than the previous one.
options.feedback: Sentence length is a matter of style and has no bearing on the argument.

options.text: Every paragraph should contain a question.
options.feedback: A paragraph may ask a rhetorical question, but that is not a requirement.

options.text: Every claim should avoid the use of connectives.
options.feedback: Connectives are what make the relationships between claims visible, and avoiding them weakens the writing.

questions.explanation:
An argument is a chain of supported claims. Without support the text is a list of opinions.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sequence best describes the movement of a well-built argumentative paragraph?
questions.context: A student examines the internal structure of the paragraphs of a model essay.

options.text: Evidence, more evidence, and a repetition of the topic.
options.feedback: The first sequence piles up support without explaining what it supports.

options.text: Claim, explanation, evidence and a link back to the argument.
options.feedback: Correct! The sequence states the point, explains it, supports it and returns to the whole argument.

options.text: Question, answer, question and answer with no position.
options.feedback: The third sequence offers a series of exchanges and never states a position.

options.text: Definition, example, definition and example.
options.feedback: The fourth sequence is a pattern of illustration with no argument in it.

questions.explanation:
Each part of a paragraph has a function, and the order lets the reader follow the reasoning from the claim to the support.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly attributes an opinion to a group rather than to the writer?
questions.context: A student writes an essay in which a professional opinion has to be reported rather than asserted.

options.text: The measure will not reduce costs.
options.feedback: The first sentence asserts the claim in the writer's own voice.

options.text: I think the measure will not reduce costs.
options.feedback: The second sentence is a personal opinion, which is a different thing.

options.text: Economists argue that the measure will not reduce costs.
options.feedback: Correct! The sentence names who holds the view, so the reader can tell the opinion from the writer's own claim.

options.text: It is clear that costs will not fall.
options.feedback: The fourth sentence presents the claim as a fact and hides the source.

questions.explanation:
Reporting an opinion and holding it are two different acts, and the verb plus the subject make the difference visible.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence would make a weak argument appear stronger than it is?
questions.context: A student identifies an overstated claim in a draft essay.

options.text: The proposal reduces costs by a measured amount.
options.feedback: The first sentence is supported by measurement and is strong for a reason.

options.text: The proposal may reduce costs slightly.
options.feedback: The second sentence is a careful hedge and is honest about the size of the effect.

options.text: The proposal is cheaper than the alternative.
options.feedback: The third sentence is a limited comparison that does not overstate the case.

options.text: Everyone knows that the proposal is the only solution.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Everyone knows' and 'the only solution' claim universal agreement and exclusivity without any evidence.

questions.explanation:
Absolute language is what makes a weak argument look strong. Real evidence allows a measured claim, and a measured claim persuades more readers.
---
questions.subject: ingles
